label: Purpura and non-blanching lesions
q: Is this platelet failure, vessel inflammation, or occlusion?
lead: Diascopy first: press a glass slide over the lesion. If it does not blanch, it is purpura. Then decide whether it is palpable. Flat purpura is a platelet or vessel-wall fragility problem; palpable purpura is inflammation of the vessel; retiform, branching purpura with necrosis is occlusion, and occlusion is the pattern with the shortest fuse.

stop.a: Meningococcemia or another cause of sepsis with DIC. Parenteral antibiotics immediately — before lumbar puncture, before imaging, before the rash evolves. This is the single highest-mortality decision in dermatology.

stop.l: Rapidly extending geographic purpura with dusky centers
stop.a: Purpura fulminans. Blood cultures, coagulation screen, and treat for sepsis. Mortality is high and hours matter.

Occlusive vasculopathy: DIC, calciphylaxis, warfarin or heparin necrosis, antiphospholipid syndrome, cholesterol embolization, or levamisole-adulterated cocaine. Biopsy the edge and screen for the cause. This pattern is not vasculitis and steroids are not the answer.

stop.l: Purpura with hematuria, red cell casts, or new hypertension
stop.a: Renal vasculitis. Urgent urinalysis with microscopy, creatinine, and nephrology referral. Irreversible renal damage develops quickly and silently.

stop.l: Purpura with abdominal pain and bloody stools in a child
stop.a: IgA vasculitis with bowel involvement. Watch for intussusception. Admit if the pain is significant.

stop.l: Extensive spontaneous bruising with mucosal bleeding
stop.a: Severe thrombocytopenia. Urgent FBC and film. Withhold aspirin, NSAIDs and intramuscular injections.

stop.l: Purpura with hemoptysis, hematuria or red-cell casts
stop.a: Suspect ANCA-associated vasculitis with pulmonary-renal involvement. Check ANCA, urinalysis and renal function and refer urgently - this is a medical emergency.

stop.l: Fever with petechiae that began on the wrists, ankles, palms or soles after outdoor exposure
stop.a: Rocky Mountain spotted fever or another rickettsiosis. Start doxycycline immediately, at any age including young children, and do not wait for serology, which is negative in the first week. Mortality is driven almost entirely by treatment started after day 5, and 40% never recall a tick bite.

stop.l: New skin necrosis with a platelet count that has halved 5 to 10 days after starting heparin
stop.a: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Stop all heparin including line flushes and coated catheters, start a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban or fondaparinux), and send PF4 antibodies. This is a prothrombotic emergency - do not transfuse platelets and do not start warfarin alone.

dx.look: Palpable purpura, retiform purpura, nodules or ulcers as the skin sign of a systemic small-to-medium-vessel vasculitis; look for the pulmonary-renal syndrome (hemoptysis, nephritis), sinonasal disease in GPA, or asthma with eosinophilia in EGPA.
fr: Palpable or retiform purpura with systemic features
Sinonasal disease, saddle-nose or lung nodules (GPA)
Asthma, eosinophilia and neuropathy (EGPA)
Hematuria, red-cell casts or a rising creatinine
Constitutional symptoms - fever, weight loss
ag: Purely cutaneous disease in a well patient
Lesions confined to dependent areas with an obvious trigger
dx.cf: Check ANCA (PR3 and MPO by ELISA), urinalysis with microscopy, renal function and chest imaging, and biopsy for vasculitis; ANCA-associated disease with lung or kidney involvement is an emergency.
dx.hp: Leukocytoclastic (and in GPA/EGPA granulomatous) vasculitis of small-to-medium vessels; tissue is often pauci-immune on direct immunofluorescence.
dx.assoc: The pulmonary-renal syndrome is the danger - check ANCA (PR3/MPO), urinalysis with microscopy, renal function and chest imaging; a positive ANCA with organ involvement is a medical emergency.
dx.mgmt: Urgent rheumatology or nephrology referral; induction with rituximab or cyclophosphamide plus corticosteroids for organ-threatening disease. This is not a skin-limited problem.

dx.look: A medium-vessel vasculitis producing tender subcutaneous nodules, livedo racemosa, retiform purpura and punched-out ulcers, typically on the lower legs; the cutaneous-limited form spares viscera, while systemic disease causes mononeuritis multiplex, renal and GI involvement.
fr: Tender dermal or subcutaneous nodules along livedo racemosa
Punched-out ulcers and retiform purpura on the legs
Mononeuritis multiplex (foot or wrist drop)
Association with hepatitis B in the systemic form
Myalgia, hypertension and constitutional symptoms in systemic disease
dx.cf: A deep (wedge or incisional) biopsy is needed to capture the medium-sized artery at the dermal-subcutaneous junction; check hepatitis B serology and assess for systemic involvement.
dx.hp: Necrotizing vasculitis of a medium-sized muscular artery at the dermal-subcutaneous junction with fibrinoid necrosis - a deep biopsy is essential to capture it.
dx.assoc: Check hepatitis B serology (a recognized trigger of systemic disease) and assess for neuropathy, renal and GI involvement; the cutaneous-limited form has a better prognosis.
dx.mgmt: Cutaneous-limited disease - NSAIDs, colchicine or low-dose corticosteroids; systemic disease - high-dose corticosteroids with cyclophosphamide, plus antiviral therapy if hepatitis B-associated.

dx.look: Palpable purpura: bright red to purple, well-demarcated macules and papules with a central hemorrhagic dot, symmetric and concentrated on the lower legs and ankles where stasis aggravates them. May become hemorrhagic bullae, necrose and ulcerate. Idiopathic in about half; drug or infection in most of the rest.
fr: Palpable, not merely visible
Lower legs and ankles, symmetric, worse with dependency
New drug or infection in the preceding weeks
Lesions of differing ages in crops
Burning or pain rather than itch
ag: Purely in sun-damaged forearm skin of an elderly patient
dx.cf: Biopsy a lesion 24–48 hours old for histology, plus a second specimen for direct immunofluorescence. Then FBC, renal function, urinalysis, ANCA, ANA, complement, cryoglobulins, and hepatitis B and C serology.
dx.hp: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis of postcapillary venules - a neutrophilic infiltrate with karyorrhexis, fibrinoid necrosis and extravasated red cells; send a specimen for direct immunofluorescence.
dx.assoc: Palpable purpura on dependent areas; seek a trigger (infection, drug, connective-tissue disease, malignancy) and check urinalysis and renal function for systemic involvement.
dx.mgmt: Remove the trigger; leg elevation and supportive care for skin-limited disease; colchicine, dapsone or systemic steroids for persistent or systemic disease.

dx.look: Mainly children, most after an upper respiratory infection, often streptococcal. Palpable purpura on buttocks and extensor legs, with colicky abdominal pain worse after meals, arthritis of knees and ankles, and renal involvement with hematuria and red cell casts. IgA on immunofluorescence.
fr: Child or adolescent
Buttocks and extensor legs
Preceding upper respiratory infection
Colicky abdominal pain, worse after eating
Arthralgia of knees and ankles
Hematuria
ag: Older adult with no systemic features
dx.cf: Biopsy with direct immunofluorescence showing vascular IgA is diagnostic. Urinalysis at presentation and repeatedly for 6 months — nephritis can appear late and is the determinant of long-term outcome.
dx.hp: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis with perivascular IgA deposition on direct immunofluorescence - the defining feature.
dx.assoc: Often post-infectious in children; watch for the tetrad of palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain and nephritis - monitor blood pressure and urinalysis for renal involvement.
dx.mgmt: Supportive care (most resolve); analgesia for joints; corticosteroids for severe abdominal or renal disease, with nephrology follow-up.

dx.look: Fever with an evolving purpuric eruption. Early: discrete pink-purple macules and papules. Later: geographic gray-black cutaneous infarction with sharp irregular borders, hemorrhagic bullae and gangrene of acral parts. Schistocytes on film, low platelets, prolonged clotting times.
fr: Fever, rigors, systemic toxicity
Lesions evolving over hours, not days
Geographic infarcts with sharp irregular borders
Acrocyanosis of fingers, toes, nose, ears
Thrombocytopenia with prolonged PT and low fibrinogen
dx.cf: Blood cultures and a coagulation screen, but do not wait for either — give parenteral antibiotics now. Gram stain of a pustule or aspirate can show organisms in acute meningococcemia within minutes.
dx.hp: Vascular thrombosis with neutrophilic vessel damage and organisms; a Gram stain and blood cultures are the priority, not histology.
dx.assoc: Retiform or stellate purpura with fever and hypotension - a medical emergency; draw blood cultures and check coagulation and platelets for DIC.
dx.mgmt: Do not wait for tests - give empiric parenteral antibiotics immediately and resuscitate; escalate to critical care.

dx.look: Strictly macular, non-palpable petechiae and ecchymoses, dependent areas and sites of minor trauma, with mucosal bleeding — gums, epistaxis, menorrhagia. Immune, drug-induced, marrow failure or consumptive.
fr: Flat, impalpable petechiae
Mucosal bleeding: gums, nose, heavy periods
Recent new drug, especially heparin, quinine or a sulfonamide
Widespread rather than confined to the legs
ag: Lesions confined to an inflamed area
dx.cf: FBC with a blood film. The film is essential: it separates immune thrombocytopenia from a consumptive microangiopathy (schistocytes) and from pseudothrombocytopenia due to EDTA clumping.
dx.hp: Biopsy is done only to exclude vasculitis when palpability is in doubt - the diagnosis is made on the platelet count and blood film. It shows extravasated red cells in the dermis with no vessel-wall inflammation, no fibrinoid necrosis and no nuclear dust.
dx.assoc: Non-palpable (macular) purpura with a low platelet count; a peripheral smear separates immune thrombocytopenia from a consumptive microangiopathy (TTP or DIC, with schistocytes), which is an emergency.
dx.mgmt: Treat the underlying cause; urgent hematology referral for microangiopathy or severe thrombocytopenia.

dx.look: Chronic, asymptomatic or mildly itchy, cayenne-pepper petechiae on a golden-brown background of hemosiderin, on the lower legs. Slowly progressive over months to years. Capillaritis, not vasculitis, and entirely benign.
fr: Cayenne-pepper speckling on a golden-brown ground
Present for months without systemic symptoms
Confined to the lower legs
Non-palpable
dx.cf: Clinical. Biopsy only if the picture is atypical or if mycosis fungoides is a consideration — lichenoid purpura can be an early expression of MF. Reassurance, compression and topical steroid are usually all that is needed.
dx.dsc: A coppery-red background with round to oval red dots and globules (extravasation and hemosiderin) - a useful separator from vasculitis.
dx.hp: Lymphocytic capillaritis - perivascular lymphocytes, extravasated red cells and hemosiderin without fibrinoid necrosis.
dx.assoc: Benign and chronic; confirm the platelet count is normal. A rare mycosis-fungoides-like variant exists - biopsy persistent or atypical cases.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance; a topical corticosteroid for itch and leg compression for support; the discoloration fades slowly.

dx.look: Recurrent palpable purpura on the legs, worse in the cold, with arthralgia and weakness. In type I, hyperviscosity and acral necrosis and digital gangrene. Types II and III are strongly associated with hepatitis C.
fr: Purpura precipitated or worsened by cold
Arthralgia with weakness
Hepatitis C infection
Peripheral neuropathy
Low C4 with normal or near-normal C3
ag: Normal complement and negative hepatitis serology
dx.cf: Serum cryoglobulins, which must be transported to the laboratory at 37 °C or the result will be falsely negative. Plus hepatitis C serology and RNA, complement, rheumatoid factor, and serum protein electrophoresis.
dx.hp: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis, often with intraluminal hyaline (cryoglobulin) thrombi in the type I form.
dx.assoc: Retiform or palpable purpura on dependent and cold-exposed sites; send serum cryoglobulins on a warm-kept sample, plus complement and hepatitis C - the leading cause of mixed cryoglobulinemia.
dx.mgmt: Treat the driver (direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C); immunosuppression (rituximab, corticosteroids) and plasma exchange for severe systemic disease.

dx.look: Scattered, asymmetric purpuric or pustulopurpuric lesions on acral sites, with Janeway lesions (painless palmar macules), Osler nodes (painful pulp nodules), splinter hemorrhages and Roth spots, alongside fever and a new murmur.
fr: Fever with a new or changed murmur
Acral, asymmetric, scattered distribution
Splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions
Prosthetic valve, injecting drug use, recent dental work
dx.cf: Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics, plus transthoracic and then transesophageal echocardiography. Apply the modified Duke criteria.
dx.hp: Vessel occlusion by septic thrombi with a neutrophilic infiltrate and organisms; culture the blood and any lesion.
dx.assoc: Acral petechiae, Janeway lesions and Osler nodes with fever - draw blood cultures and obtain an echocardiogram; search for a source and for embolic phenomena elsewhere.
dx.mgmt: Admit for blood cultures, echocardiography and prompt intravenous antibiotics per endocarditis protocols; involve cardiology and infectious diseases.

dx.look: Exquisitely painful retiform purpura progressing to black eschar and ulceration, on adipose-rich sites — thighs, abdomen, buttocks. Almost always in end-stage renal disease on dialysis. Pain is out of all proportion and precedes visible change.
fr: End-stage renal disease, dialysis, or a renal transplant
Pain far exceeding the visible lesion
Adipose-rich sites: thighs, abdomen, breasts
Retiform branching outline with central necrosis
Warfarin use, raised calcium-phosphate product
dx.cf: Deep incisional biopsy shows calcification of the media of small dermal and subcutaneous vessels with intimal fibroplasia. Biopsy carries a real risk of creating a non-healing ulcer, so weigh it. Mortality approaches 50% at one year.
dx.hp: Calcification of the media of small dermal and subcutaneous arterioles with intimal fibrosis, thrombosis and fat necrosis.
dx.assoc: End-stage renal disease or dialysis; check calcium, phosphate and PTH. Warfarin and obesity are risk factors. Retiform purpura is intensely painful and progresses to necrosis.
dx.mgmt: Aggressive wound care and analgesia; sodium thiosulfate, correction of the calcium-phosphate product, and multidisciplinary care; avoid warfarin and calcium-based binders.

dx.look: Sharply demarcated dark purple non-palpable macules on the extensor forearms and dorsal hands of an older adult, on a background of solar elastosis and atrophy, often with white stellate pseudoscars. Resolves over weeks without the color change of a true bruise.
fr: Extensor forearms and dorsal hands only
Marked background photodamage and skin atrophy
Long-term topical or systemic corticosteroid use
No systemic symptoms
Recurs with minor knocks
dx.cf: Clinical, and needs no investigation. Recognizing it prevents a cascade of unnecessary vasculitis screening in a well older patient.
dx.hp: Dermal solar elastosis with extravasated red cells; biopsy is not needed.
dx.assoc: Chronic sun-damaged, thin skin on the dorsal forearms of older adults; worsened by anticoagulants and by chronic topical or systemic steroids - review the medication list.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance and skin protection; there is no specific treatment, though photoprotection limits progression.

dx.look: A triad confined to the ankles and lower legs: livedo racemosa, ivory-white stellate scars (atrophie blanche) ringed by telangiectasia and hemosiderin, and small punched-out ulcers that hurt far more than their size suggests. Lesions start as focal retiform purpura, ulcerate, and heal slowly into porcelain-white scars. Flares recur in summer and winter over years.
fr: Ankles and lower legs only, bilateral
Ivory-white stellate scars with surrounding telangiectasia
Small punched-out ulcers with pain out of proportion to size
Recurrent seasonal flares over years
Atrophie blanche without varicose veins to explain it
Ulcers that heal over months, not weeks
ag: Lesions above the knee or on the trunk
dx.cf: Biopsy the edge of a fresh purpuric lesion, deep enough to reach the reticular dermis: hyaline fibrin thrombi with wedge-shaped infarction and hyalinized vessel walls, and no true vasculitis. Then screen for thrombophilia - antiphospholipid antibodies, factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein C and S, antithrombin, homocysteine and cryofibrinogen.
dx.hp: Segmental hyalinizing vasculopathy - fibrin thrombi in small dermal vessels with hyalinized walls and wedge-shaped dermal necrosis, without neutrophilic vessel-wall destruction.
dx.assoc: About half have an identifiable thrombophilia; antiphospholipid syndrome, Sneddon syndrome and hyperhomocysteinemia are the ones worth chasing. Recognizing this as occlusion rather than inflammation is what prevents years of futile immunosuppression.
dx.mgmt: Anticoagulation is the treatment - low-molecular-weight heparin or a direct oral anticoagulant, with antiplatelet therapy and pentoxifylline. Stop smoking, give real analgesia, and reserve corticosteroids for pain relief rather than control. Compression only after arterial assessment.

dx.look: Broken, irregular, branching livedo racemosa on the trunk and limbs that does not reverse on warming, with retiform purpura, splinter hemorrhages, painful leg ulcers and frank skin necrosis. The history carries the diagnosis: prior arterial or venous thrombosis, or recurrent fetal loss. The catastrophic form produces widespread cutaneous infarction with multiorgan failure over days.
fr: Prior deep vein thrombosis, stroke or arterial occlusion
Three or more first-trimester miscarriages, or a late fetal loss
Broken, irregular livedo racemosa that persists on warming
Mild thrombocytopenia with a prolonged aPTT
Known lupus or another connective tissue disease
Retiform purpura with no fever and no inflammatory markers
ag: Regular, fully reversible net-like livedo in a young woman with cold hands
Repeatedly negative antibodies on samples 12 weeks apart
Purely inflammatory palpable purpura with a raised CRP
dx.cf: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I antibodies (IgG and IgM), repeated after 12 weeks - a single positive result does not make the diagnosis, and transient positives follow infection. Biopsy shows bland thrombosis without vasculitis.
dx.hp: Noninflammatory thrombosis of dermal and subcutaneous vessels; there is no fibrinoid vessel-wall necrosis and no neutrophilic infiltrate, which is what separates it from vasculitis.
dx.assoc: Primary, or secondary to lupus. It drives stroke, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism and obstetric loss, so making the diagnosis changes management for life. Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome carries a mortality near 50% and needs anticoagulation, corticosteroids and plasma exchange started the same day.
dx.mgmt: Refer to hematology or rheumatology. Lifelong warfarin after thrombosis - direct oral anticoagulants are inferior in triple-positive disease. Low-dose aspirin with low-molecular-weight heparin in pregnancy. Treat cardiovascular risk factors and stop estrogen-containing contraception.

dx.look: Warfarin necrosis appears on days 3 to 5 of therapy as a painful red plaque on a fat-rich site - breast, buttock, thigh, abdomen, calf - which becomes purple-black and demarcates into a full-thickness infarct with sharp borders; acral sites are spared. Heparin necrosis appears as retiform purpura and necrosis at subcutaneous injection sites, or at distant sites when it accompanies heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
fr: Onset on days 3 to 5 of warfarin, especially after a large loading dose
Adipose-rich sites - breast, buttock, thigh, abdomen - with acral sparing
Necrosis at heparin injection sites
Platelet count fallen by more than half, 5 to 10 days after starting heparin
Known protein C, protein S or antithrombin deficiency
Sharply demarcated purple-black infarct on a red base
ag: Stable anticoagulation for months or years before onset
Lesions confined to the lower legs in a dependent pattern
A stable platelet count throughout heparin exposure
dx.cf: Clinical, on the drug timeline and the site. Check the platelet trend and calculate a 4T score before sending heparin-PF4 antibodies; send protein C and S activity, remembering that warfarin itself lowers both. Biopsy shows fibrin thrombi in dermal and subcutaneous vessels with no vasculitis.
dx.hp: Fibrin thrombi occluding dermal and subcutaneous venules with hemorrhage and full-thickness necrosis, and no inflammatory vessel-wall damage.
dx.assoc: Warfarin necrosis reflects a transient hypercoagulable window as protein C, which has a short half-life, falls before factors II, IX and X. Heparin necrosis is a marker of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which is a prothrombotic emergency and not a bleeding one - up to half develop new thrombosis.
dx.mgmt: Stop the drug. For warfarin necrosis give vitamin K with heparin cover and continue anticoagulation by another route, adding protein C concentrate or fresh frozen plasma in protein C deficiency. For suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia stop all heparin including line flushes and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban or fondaparinux - never platelet transfusion, never warfarin alone. Debride and graft established necrosis.

dx.look: Perifollicular hemorrhage around keratin-plugged follicles on the lower legs, with fragmented, coiled corkscrew hairs buried in the hyperkeratotic papules. Larger ecchymoses follow and can become generalized. Gums are swollen, purple, spongy, bleed easily and let teeth loosen. Fatigue, arthralgia and myalgia come first, and the leg pain is from subperiosteal bleeding.
fr: Perifollicular purpura with follicular hyperkeratosis on the legs
Coiled corkscrew hairs within the papules
Swollen, spongy, bleeding gums with loose teeth
Alcohol dependence, isolation, food faddism or an edentulous diet
Fatigue, arthralgia and myalgia preceding the rash
Splinter hemorrhages and poor wound healing
ag: A varied diet including fresh fruit and vegetables
Healthy gums with normal wound healing
dx.cf: Serum ascorbic acid is low to zero, but the assay is fragile and rarely available quickly, so a therapeutic trial is diagnostic: spontaneous bleeding stops within 24 hours and gum bleeding within 2 to 3 days. Check the platelet count and clotting screen in parallel, since they are normal here and abnormal in the main alternatives.
dx.dsc: Red perifollicular halos of hemorrhage around keratin-plugged follicles, with coiled corkscrew hairs inside the papules - visible on dermoscopy well before the diagnosis is usually considered.
dx.hp: Perifollicular hemorrhage with keratin plugging and coiled hairs within the follicular infundibulum; vessels are structurally normal and there is no vasculitis.
dx.assoc: Alcohol dependence, homelessness, psychiatric illness, food faddism, isolated older adults, restrictive diets after bariatric surgery, and pregnancy or lactation. Coexisting folate and iron deficiency are usual. Untreated scurvy is fatal from intracerebral or subarachnoid hemorrhage, which is why this cheap diagnosis matters.
dx.mgmt: Ascorbic acid 100 mg three to five times daily until 4 g has been given, then 100 mg daily, with dietary correction and treatment of coexisting deficiencies. Rapid improvement in bleeding and bone pain is expected and confirms the diagnosis.
dx.pat: Perifollicular on legs, with gum bleeding

dx.look: Purpura appearing in skin that has merely been pinched, rubbed, coughed or strained against - eyelids and periorbital skin, neck, axillae, umbilicus, body folds and anogenital area - on skin that otherwise looks normal or carries smooth, waxy, translucent papules and nodules. Complete the picture with a firm woody macroglossia showing dental indentations, nail dystrophy and carpal tunnel syndrome.
fr: Periorbital purpura after pinching, rubbing, coughing or vomiting
Smooth waxy translucent papules in folds and around the eyes
Macroglossia, firm and woody, with lateral tooth indentations
Carpal tunnel syndrome, neuropathy or unexplained heart failure
Nephrotic-range proteinuria
Fatigue, weight loss and dyspnea
ag: A single episode with obvious preceding trauma
Purpura confined to the lower legs
Normal serum free light chain ratio with negative immunofixation
dx.cf: Serum free light chains with serum and urine immunofixation detect the plasma cell clone in nearly all cases. Confirm amyloid with Congo red staining showing apple-green birefringence on lesional skin or an abdominal fat-pad aspirate, then type the deposits and assess cardiac, renal and hepatic involvement.
dx.hp: Faintly eosinophilic amyloid masses in the papillary and reticular dermis, in sweat glands and within vessel walls; Congo red gives apple-green birefringence under polarized light and immunohistochemistry shows light chain restriction.
dx.assoc: Plasma cell dyscrasia or myeloma. Cardiac involvement determines survival, so check NT-proBNP, troponin and an echocardiogram at diagnosis. Amyloid in the vessel wall is why trivial pressure produces purpura, and acquired factor X deficiency can compound the bleeding.
dx.mgmt: Urgent hematology referral. Treatment targets the plasma cell clone - daratumumab with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide and dexamethasone, with autologous stem cell transplant in selected cases. The skin sign is the cheap early clue, and outcome depends on how quickly the heart is assessed.

dx.n: Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other rickettsioses
dx.look: Abrupt fever, shaking rigors, severe headache and myalgia, then on day 3 to 5 pink 2 to 6 mm blanching macules beginning on the wrists, forearms and ankles and spreading centripetally to arms, thighs, trunk and face, involving palms and soles. Within 2 to 4 days the lesions become hemorrhagic and stop blanching. An inoculation eschar occurs in most other spotted fevers but not in Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
fr: Rash starting on wrists and ankles and spreading centrally
Palms and soles involved
Fever, severe headache, myalgia and photophobia preceding the rash
Tick exposure or outdoor activity in an endemic area
Confusion, stupor or seizures
Thrombocytopenia with hyponatremia and raised transaminases
ag: No possible exposure within the last month
dx.cf: Treat first and confirm later. The diagnosis is clinical and epidemiologic in the first days: only 3% present with the full triad of rash, fever and a recalled tick bite, and 40% never recall a bite at all. Paired acute and convalescent immunofluorescent antibody titers confirm it retrospectively, and immunohistochemistry on a punch biopsy of a purpuric lesion can confirm it early.
dx.hp: Rickettsiae multiply in endothelial cells, producing a lymphohistiocytic vasculitis with vessel thrombosis, necrosis and extravasated red cells; immunohistochemistry on lesional skin detects the organism.
dx.assoc: Rickettsia rickettsii transmitted by dog and wood ticks. Mortality concentrates in those treated after day 5, and is higher in older men, in alcohol dependence and in G6PD deficiency. Complications are acral gangrene, acute kidney injury and encephalitis. Spotless disease occurs in up to 10% and carries a higher mortality because the diagnosis is made late.
dx.mgmt: Doxycycline started on clinical suspicion at any age - 100 mg twice daily in adults and children over 45 kg, 2.2 mg/kg per dose twice daily (maximum 100 mg) in children under 45 kg. The risk of untreated disease far exceeds the risk of dental staining from one course. Defervescence within 48 to 72 hours supports the diagnosis. Do not substitute a beta-lactam.

ctx.s: IgA vasculitis is predominantly a pediatric disease, Fitzpatrick 8e §14
Fever transforms this presentation into an emergency, Fitzpatrick 8e §25

ctx.l: End-stage renal disease or on dialysis
New drug in the last 6 weeks

ctx.s: 75% of IgA vasculitis follows an upper respiratory infection, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

ctx.l: Injecting drug use or prosthetic heart valve

ctx.s: Warfarin is a recognized risk factor for calciphylaxis, Fitzpatrick 8e §19

ctx.l: Alcohol dependence, homelessness, or a diet without fresh fruit and vegetables
ctx.s: Scurvy is most common in alcoholism and in isolated edentulous adults, Fitzpatrick 8e §15

ctx.l: Started or reloaded an anticoagulant in the last 10 days
ctx.s: Warfarin necrosis appears on days 3 to 5; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia at days 5 to 10, Fitzpatrick 8e §23

find.l: Lesions are palpable
find.s: Palpability is the classic separator of vasculitic from platelet purpura, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Retiform, branching or net-like outline
find.s: Retiform purpura indicates vessel occlusion rather than inflammation, Fitzpatrick 8e §20

find.l: Fever with systemic toxicity
Lesions evolving visibly over hours
find.s: Rapid evolution is characteristic of purpura fulminans, Fitzpatrick 8e §20

find.l: Symmetric on lower legs and ankles, worse with dependency
find.s: Stasis-dependent distribution of small vessel vasculitis, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Buttocks and extensor legs in a child
Colicky abdominal pain, worse after meals
find.s: Bowel angina in IgA vasculitis, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Hematuria or red cell casts on urinalysis
Mucosal bleeding: gums, epistaxis, menorrhagia
Confined to extensor forearms and dorsal hands with photodamage
Cayenne-pepper speckling on a golden-brown background
Pain far out of proportion to the visible lesion
find.s: Disproportionate pain is the earliest sign of calciphylaxis, Fitzpatrick 8e §19

find.l: Precipitated or worsened by cold
New or changed cardiac murmur
Splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes or Janeway lesions
Acral necrosis or digital gangrene
Purpura with hematuria, red-cell casts or pulmonary symptoms
Tender subcutaneous nodules along livedo racemosa with punched-out ulcers
Ivory-white stellate scars (atrophie blanche) around the ankles
Small punched-out ankle ulcers recurring every summer and winter for years
find.s: Livedo reticularis with winter and summer ulceration, Fitzpatrick 8e §17

find.l: Prior arterial or venous thrombosis, or recurrent fetal loss
Prolonged aPTT that does not correct on mixing, or a false-positive syphilis serology
Sharply demarcated purple-black infarct on breast, buttock, thigh or abdomen
find.s: Warfarin necrosis spares acral sites and favors fat-rich areas, Fitzpatrick 8e §23

find.l: Necrosis at heparin injection sites, or a platelet count halved since starting heparin
find.s: Heparin necrosis and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, Fitzpatrick 8e §23

find.l: Perifollicular purpura with coiled corkscrew hairs on the legs
Swollen, spongy, bleeding gums with loosening teeth
Purpura around the eyes or in folds appearing after pinching, coughing or straining
find.s: Pinch purpura in systemic AL amyloidosis, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Waxy translucent papules, macroglossia or carpal tunnel syndrome with the purpura
Rash began on wrists and ankles and spread centrally, involving palms and soles
find.s: Centripetal spread from wrists and ankles is specific to Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Fitzpatrick 8e §25

find.l: Tick exposure or outdoor activity in an endemic area in the last 2 weeks
find.s: Only 60% recall a preceding tick bite, Fitzpatrick 8e §25

find.l: Mononeuritis multiplex with foot drop or wrist drop alongside the skin lesions
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14 - mixed motor and sensory mononeuritis multiplex in polyarteritis nodosa

find.l: Chronic sinonasal crusting or septal perforation, or asthma with blood eosinophilia
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - upper airway disease in GPA and asthma with eosinophilia in EGPA

test.l: ANCA (PR3 and MPO by ELISA) with urinalysis and renal function
test.w: Palpable or retiform purpura with any systemic feature - sinonasal, pulmonary, renal or neurologic.
test.p: A positive PR3 or MPO ANCA with organ involvement supports ANCA-associated vasculitis. Refer urgently for immunosuppression.
test.n: A negative ANCA does not exclude vasculitis - biopsy for histology and reassess; ANCA can be negative in limited disease.
test.x: ANCA can be positive in other settings (cocaine or levamisole, endocarditis, drugs); confirm by ELISA and correlate clinically.

test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e Introduction — pressing a glass slide separates erythema from extravasated blood
test.w: Before anything else, on every red lesion in this presentation. It costs nothing and it decides which branch of the differential you are in.
test.p: Failure to blanch confirms extravasated blood. You are dealing with purpura, not erythema. Now decide whether it is palpable.
test.n: Blanching means erythema, and the differential is a different one entirely — urticaria, cellulitis, drug eruption.
test.x: Diascopy also reveals the glassy apple-jelly nodules of sarcoidosis, lupus vulgaris and granuloma annulare. Use it more widely than for purpura alone.

test.l: FBC with blood film, coagulation screen
test.w: Every patient with purpura. It is the fastest way to separate the platelet disorders from the vasculitides, and it is the test that finds a consumptive microangiopathy before it is clinically obvious.
test.p: Isolated thrombocytopenia points to immune or drug-induced disease. Schistocytes with low platelets and prolonged clotting indicate DIC or a thrombotic microangiopathy — that is a hematologic emergency.
test.n: A normal platelet count with normal clotting in palpable purpura points firmly to vasculitis and directs you to biopsy.
test.x: Ask specifically for a film. An automated count alone will miss schistocytes, and will report EDTA-induced platelet clumping as genuine thrombocytopenia.

test.l: Lesional biopsy (24–48 h old) plus direct immunofluorescence
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14 — all purpuric lesions should be biopsied
test.w: Any palpable purpura. Take two specimens: one in formalin for histology, one in Michel medium for immunofluorescence.
test.p: Fibrinoid necrosis of postcapillary venules with neutrophils and nuclear dust confirms leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Vascular IgA on immunofluorescence makes it IgA vasculitis, which changes the follow-up.
test.n: A negative biopsy from a lesion older than 48 hours is uninterpretable. Sample a fresh lesion.
test.x: The immunofluorescence window is narrower than the histology window — IgA deposits degrade after about 48 hours. If you can only take one specimen from an old lesion, take histology and accept the limitation.

test.l: Blood cultures before antibiotics, with Gram stain of a lesion
test.w: Any purpura with fever. Take the cultures, then give the antibiotics — but if taking cultures would delay treatment by more than a few minutes, treat first.
test.p: Identifies the organism and directs therapy. Gram-negative diplococci on a lesional Gram stain confirms meningococcemia within minutes.
test.n: Negative cultures do not exclude meningococcemia, particularly after any antibiotic exposure. Continue treatment on clinical grounds.
test.x: This is the one situation in dermatology where the diagnostic pathway must not delay treatment. The purpura of meningococcemia can progress from a few macules to fatal purpura fulminans within hours.

test.w: Every patient with palpable purpura, at presentation, and repeatedly for 6 months in IgA vasculitis.
test.p: Red cell casts or proteinuria indicate glomerular involvement. Refer to nephrology — renal disease determines the long-term outcome and progresses silently.
test.n: A normal urinalysis at presentation does not exclude later nephritis. In IgA vasculitis, nephritis can appear weeks after the rash has cleared, which is why the follow-up schedule matters more than the initial result.
test.x: Dipstick alone is not sufficient. Ask for microscopy — casts are the finding that changes management.

test.w: Recurrent purpura worsened by cold, especially with hepatitis C, neuropathy or a low C4.
test.p: Confirms cryoglobulinemia. Type and quantify, then treat the underlying cause — in types II and III that usually means hepatitis C.
test.n: A negative result is unreliable if the specimen cooled in transit, which is the commonest reason for a false negative.
test.x: Warn the laboratory in advance. The sample must be collected in a pre-warmed tube and kept at 37 °C until the serum is separated, or the cryoglobulin precipitates and is discarded with the clot.

test.l: Deep incisional biopsy for medial calcification
test.w: Retiform purpura with disproportionate pain in a dialysis patient, when the diagnosis will change management.
test.p: Calcification of the media of small vessels with intimal fibroplasia and thrombosis confirms calciphylaxis. Involve nephrology, correct the calcium-phosphate product, stop warfarin, and consider sodium thiosulfate.
test.n: Sampling error is common because the changes are patchy. A negative biopsy in a convincing clinical picture should not overturn the diagnosis.
test.x: The biopsy itself can create a non-healing ulcer at a site that will not heal. Weigh that cost honestly, and consider treating on clinical grounds when the setting is characteristic.

test.l: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I antibodies
test.w: Retiform purpura or livedo racemosa with any thrombotic or obstetric history, unexplained leg ulcers, or a prolonged aPTT in someone who is not bleeding.
test.p: Persistent positivity confirms antiphospholipid syndrome and commits to lifelong anticoagulation after a thrombotic event, and to aspirin with heparin in pregnancy. Triple positivity carries the highest risk.
test.n: A negative panel does not exclude the syndrome during acute thrombosis or while on anticoagulation, both of which interfere with lupus anticoagulant assays. Retest when stable.
test.x: The result must be confirmed on a second sample at least 12 weeks later. Transient positives after infection are common, and acting on a single result commits someone to lifelong warfarin they may not need.

test.l: Serum ascorbic acid with an empiric therapeutic trial of vitamin C
test.w: Perifollicular purpura on the legs, corkscrew hairs, or bleeding gums in anyone with alcohol dependence, social isolation, malabsorption or a restricted diet.
test.p: An undetectable level confirms it. More usefully, bleeding stops within 24 hours and gum bleeding within 2 to 3 days of replacement, which confirms the diagnosis before the level returns.
test.n: A borderline level does not exclude tissue depletion, and recent hospital food or a single supplement dose can normalize it. Treat on the clinical picture.
test.x: The specimen is light and heat sensitive and degrades if it sits around, so a normal result from a mishandled sample is common. Do not withhold treatment while waiting - the whole point is that it is cheap, safe and curative.

test.l: Serum free light chains, immunofixation, and Congo red staining of skin or fat pad
test.w: Purpura in a pinch, cough or rub distribution, particularly periorbital; waxy papules; macroglossia; or unexplained proteinuria, neuropathy or heart failure with any purpura.
test.p: An abnormal free light chain ratio with monoclonal protein on immunofixation, plus apple-green birefringence on Congo red, confirms AL amyloidosis. Refer urgently and assess the heart the same week.
test.n: A normal free light chain ratio with negative serum and urine immunofixation makes AL amyloidosis very unlikely and redirects toward the other causes of fragile-vessel purpura.
test.x: Serum electrophoresis alone misses a substantial proportion - free light chains plus immunofixation of both serum and urine are needed. Congo red must be read under polarized light, and typing by mass spectrometry matters because treating the wrong amyloid type is useless.

test.l: Empiric doxycycline with paired acute and convalescent rickettsial serology
test.w: Any febrile purpuric or petechial eruption that began acrally, especially with headache, myalgia, thrombocytopenia or hyponatremia after outdoor exposure.
test.p: A fourfold rise in immunofluorescent antibody titer between acute and convalescent samples confirms it. Defervescence within 48 to 72 hours of doxycycline is itself strong supporting evidence.
test.n: Acute serology is negative in most cases in the first week, because antibodies take 7 to 10 days to appear. A negative acute titer must never be used to stop doxycycline.
test.x: This is the classic test that is ordered and then wrongly waited on. Start doxycycline on suspicion at any age - mortality is driven almost entirely by treatment begun after day 5, and the drug can be stopped later if serology and course prove otherwise.

test.l: Deep biopsy from the edge of a fresh lesion, with a thrombophilia screen
test.w: Painful punched-out ankle ulcers with atrophie blanche, or recurrent retiform purpura confined to the lower legs, especially without varicose veins.
test.p: Hyaline fibrin thrombi with vessel-wall hyalinization and wedge-shaped infarction, and no vasculitis, confirms livedoid vasculopathy. Treat with anticoagulation and screen for thrombophilia.
test.n: A sample from an old ulcer base shows only nonspecific change. Take it from the purpuric edge of a new lesion, and repeat rather than abandon the diagnosis.
test.x: The commonest error is calling this vasculitis and treating with corticosteroids for years. If the histology shows thrombosis without vessel-wall inflammation, the answer is anticoagulation, not immunosuppression.

test.l: Platelet count trend with a 4T score and heparin-PF4 antibody testing
test.w: Any new necrotic or retiform skin lesion in someone on heparin, and any fall in platelet count of more than 50% between days 5 and 10 of exposure.
test.p: A high 4T score with positive PF4 antibodies confirms heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Stop all heparin, including flushes and coated lines, and anticoagulate with a non-heparin agent. Confirm with a functional assay where available.
test.n: A negative PF4 immunoassay with a low 4T score effectively excludes it, and heparin can continue. A positive immunoassay with a low score is often a false positive.
test.x: The dangerous instinct is to treat a falling platelet count as a bleeding problem. This is a clotting emergency - platelet transfusion and warfarin monotherapy both make it worse, and warfarin alone can precipitate venous limb gangrene.

flag: Fever plus purpura is a sepsis pathway, not a dermatology pathway, until proved otherwise. Give antibiotics first and complete the diagnostic sequence afterwards.
